## DG-PR-001

**Known payload marker in source code** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A string that appears in known PolinRider loaders (obfuscator identifiers, stage tags, XOR keys, stage-URL paths) was found in a file.

**What to do:** Do not run the project. Remove the injected code, then follow `recovery_checklist`: the machine that last ran this code may be compromised.

## DG-PR-002

**Weak payload marker** (severity: medium, campaign: polinrider)

A pattern such as `global['!']` or `global.i = 'A9-...'` that the loaders use to pass state. Rarely legitimate, but not unique, so it is rated lower on its own.

**What to do:** Inspect the surrounding code. If it sits next to obfuscated or whitespace-padded code, treat as DG-PR-001.

## DG-PR-003

**Payload hidden after whitespace padding** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A line longer than 3,000 characters contains a run of 100+ spaces or tabs followed by more code. Attackers append the payload to config files (postcss, tailwind, eslint, next, vite) after padding so it is off-screen in an editor.

**What to do:** Open the file with word wrap or `awk 'length>3000'`, remove everything after the padding, and treat the machine as exposed.

## DG-PR-004

**package.json script runs a large local JavaScript file** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A script such as `node api.js && next dev` runs a sizeable or obfuscated file before the real command. This executes the payload on every dev/build/start.

**What to do:** Remove the prefix and delete the file after confirming it is not your code.

## DG-PR-005

**VS Code task runs automatically and looks malicious** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A task with `runOn: folderOpen` runs a downloader, a shell, or `node` against a non-script file (for example a fake font). It executes when the folder is opened in a trusted VS Code workspace.

**What to do:** Delete the task, delete the file it points to, and open unknown repos in Restricted Mode.

## DG-PR-006

**VS Code task runs automatically** (severity: low, campaign: polinrider)

A task with `runOn: folderOpen` exists. Often legitimate (dev servers), but it is a known execution vector.

**What to do:** Confirm you wrote it and that it only runs code you trust.

## DG-PR-007

**Font file is not a font** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A .ttf/.otf/.woff/.woff2/.eot file does not start with a valid font header. PolinRider hides JavaScript in such files and runs it with `node`.

**What to do:** Delete the file and any task or script that references it.

## DG-PR-008

**Known attacker helper script** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

`temp_auto_push.bat` amends the latest commit with the payload, rewinds the system clock to hide the change, and force-pushes. Its presence means a machine that pushed this repo was compromised.

**What to do:** Delete it, rotate GitHub credentials, and audit recent force-pushes.

## DG-PR-009

**Heavily obfuscated JavaScript** (severity: medium, campaign: generic)

Very many `_0x....` identifiers or `\u00XX` escapes. Obfuscation is not malicious by itself (some vendors ship it), so this needs human review.

**What to do:** Check who added the file and why; compare with the upstream project.

## DG-HS-001

**Twin commits (same author, time and message; different content)** (severity: medium, campaign: polinrider)

Two commits share author, author-time and subject but have different trees. This is the fingerprint of a rewritten commit: the clean original and an amended copy that adds malware.

**What to do:** Diff the twins; treat the added files as malicious and find which machine pushed them.

## DG-HS-002

**Committer timezone re-stamped** (severity: medium, campaign: polinrider)

The committer timestamp equals the author timestamp but is written in a different timezone, by the same person. Normal workflows rarely do this; rewriting tools that reset the clock do.

**What to do:** Compare against reflogs and CI history; investigate which machine rewrote the commits.

## DG-HS-003

**Earliest commit containing a payload marker** (severity: info, campaign: polinrider)

Reports the oldest commit that adds a known marker. Commit dates are attacker-controlled and may be forged, so this shows *where* it is in history, not *when* it happened.

**What to do:** Use it to find the files to clean; do not rely on the date.

## DG-GA-001

**Workflow file name used by GhostAction** (severity: medium, campaign: ghostaction)

A workflow is named github_actions_security.yml, security-check.yml or security-audit.yml, names used by the campaign. They are also plausible legitimate names.

**What to do:** Read the file. If you did not add it, remove it and rotate every secret it can read.

## DG-GA-002

**Workflow references a known attacker host** (severity: critical, campaign: ghostaction)

The workflow mentions an IP address or domain used for secret exfiltration.

**What to do:** Remove the workflow, revoke the credential that pushed it, rotate all secrets.

## DG-GA-003

**Workflow has an exfiltration job signature** (severity: high, campaign: ghostaction)

Contains the job id `send-secrets` or step names used by GhostAction.

**What to do:** Remove the workflow and rotate all secrets the repository exposes to Actions.

## DG-GA-004

**Workflow posts secrets with curl** (severity: high, campaign: ghostaction)

A `curl` command sends `${{ secrets.X }}` values to a URL. Plain-HTTP or raw-IP targets are rated higher than HTTPS to a named host.

**What to do:** Verify the destination; if unknown, treat the secrets as stolen and rotate them.

## DG-GA-005

**Workflow scans the full git history** (severity: medium, campaign: ghostaction)

`git log -p --all` inside a workflow is how the Oct 2026 GhostAction variant harvests keys from history.

**What to do:** Confirm it is intentional (secret scanners do this); otherwise remove it.

## DG-GA-006

**Workflow serialises every secret** (severity: medium, campaign: ghostaction)

`toJSON(secrets)` exposes all repository secrets to a step.

**What to do:** Reference only the specific secrets a step needs.

## DG-GA-007

**pull_request_target checks out untrusted code** (severity: medium, campaign: ghostaction)

A `pull_request_target` workflow checks out the pull request head with access to secrets, allowing code from a fork to read them.

**What to do:** Use `pull_request`, or never check out untrusted refs in privileged workflows.

## DG-GA-008

**Commit message used by GhostAction** (severity: medium, campaign: ghostaction)

A commit message matches those used when GhostAction injects or updates its workflow, for example 'Add Github Actions Security workflow'.

**What to do:** Inspect the commit's diff and author; if you did not make it, treat it as a compromise.

## DG-MC-001

**Malware persistence directory on this machine** (severity: critical, campaign: polinrider)

`~/.node_modules` with `.npm-ws*` files is where the PolinRider runner is installed.

**What to do:** Rebuild the machine from a clean OS image and rotate every credential from a clean device.

## DG-MC-002

**Suspicious node process** (severity: critical, campaign: polinrider)

A `node -e` process that evals downloaded code or references a known marker is running.

**What to do:** Disconnect from the network, kill it, and rebuild the machine.

## DG-MC-003

**Connection to a known attacker host** (severity: critical, campaign: polinrider)

An open or recent connection to a known command-and-control address.

**What to do:** Treat the machine as compromised.

## DG-MC-004

**Suspicious startup item** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A launch agent, scheduled task, cron entry or autostart that references `.node_modules`, `node -e` or a known marker.

**What to do:** Remove it and rebuild the machine.

## DG-MC-005

**Suspicious shell startup file** (severity: high, campaign: polinrider)

A shell rc/profile file references `.node_modules`, `node -e` or a known marker.

**What to do:** Remove the line and rebuild the machine.

## DG-CR-001

**GitHub token stored in shell history** (severity: medium, campaign: generic)

A personal access token appears in a shell history file (often from `git clone https://TOKEN@github.com/...`). Infostealers read these files.

**What to do:** Revoke the token, delete the history line, and use `gh auth login` or SSH instead.

## DG-CR-002

**GitHub token embedded in a git remote URL** (severity: medium, campaign: generic)

A repository's `.git/config` contains a token in the remote URL, stored in plaintext.

**What to do:** Revoke the token and run `git remote set-url origin <clean-url>`.

## DG-CR-003

**Broad GitHub token scopes** (severity: medium, campaign: ghostaction)

The current GitHub CLI token can write workflows or administer repositories. GhostAction uses stolen tokens with the `workflow` scope to plant secret-stealing workflows.

**What to do:** Use fine-grained tokens limited to required repos and permissions; avoid `workflow`.

## DG-GH-001

**Repository Actions secrets exposure** (severity: info, campaign: ghostaction)

Lists secret *names* (never values) that a malicious workflow in this repo could read.

**What to do:** If a token with write access was ever exposed, rotate these secrets.
